title: Create large chunks of time
hook: Can 1 protected hour beat a whole day of scraps?
counterintuition: Despite how full your calendar looks, serious work rarely appears in the cracks. You create room for the frog by giving it a protected appointment.
tryThisNow: Before you start your next serious work block, spend 10 minutes counting the files, notes, and decisions you must reload; rehearse one sentence that protects the block.
keyTakeaway: Important work needs protected blocks, clear outcomes, and fewer restarts, so put your best time around the frog before the day spends it for you.

breakdown.fastRead:
Emilia blocks one hour for the proposal before her inbox opens. The task is not smaller, but the time around it is stronger. A protected work block is a scheduled stretch long enough to make real progress on one priority task. Big frogs need big rooms.

Treat the frog like an appointment with consequences. Name the outcome, protect the block, and tell people when you are unavailable. Scraps of time can handle scraps of work. Deep work needs a larger container.
breakdown.deepRead:
Files have a hidden cost. Each time Yvonne returns to a report, she has to find the spreadsheet, reopen the notes, remember the last choice, and rebuild the mental picture. Ten minutes vanish before the work even begins. A larger block saves that restart cost because the task stays warm in her hands.

That is why a calendar block works better than a strong intention. A blank hour can disappear into calls, messages, and small requests. A named block says what the hour is for: draft the proposal section, review the client files, write the decision memo. Work blocks need a named finish line.

Early time often protects the work best. Annabelle tries to write after routine demands are handled, but by then the day has learned how to interrupt her. When she moves the block before calls and messages, the hard task gets first claim on her best attention. She does not become less busy. She becomes less available to the wrong work at the wrong time.

Protection also needs other people to see it. If Ella has a blocked hour but answers every ping, the block is only a decoration. She needs a plain sentence: "I am on the client file until 11; send urgent items to the thread." The sentence is not rude. It tells the room how the work will get done.

The useful test is visible. Did a block get written on the calendar? Did it name one outcome? Did someone else know it was protected? If not, the idea stayed in your head, and the day can still spend the hour for you.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jenna sits in an onboarding room with one open laptop and three open tabs. The instructor asks the class to count how many times they restart the same file in one morning. Jenna marks five. None of the restarts looks dramatic. Each one just steals a small piece of the work.

That count changes the lesson. The problem is not only interruption. It is reentry. A complex task has context: files, notes, choices, facts, and a half-built mental map. When the map is broken into ten pieces, attention spends itself rebuilding instead of producing. One large block lets the map stay alive long enough to use it.

The block should match the frog. If the task is small, a small slot may be fine. A short email does not need a whole morning. But a proposal, plan, analysis, or hard conversation prep often needs a stretch where the mind can carry several details at once. Save your best room for your biggest frog.

There is also a social side. Ella can write "deep work" on her calendar, but if her team thinks she is free, they will keep using her as if she is free. A short note changes the setting: "I am blocked for the client files until noon; route urgent items through the project thread." The work gets a door, and the door gets a sign.

The common mistake is waiting for a large block to appear after the small work is cleared. That order rarely works. Small work breeds more small work. Messages invite replies. Calls create notes. Routine tasks can fill any space you give them. Large blocks are created, not found.

Tie the block to an outcome before it starts. "Work on strategy" is too cloudy. "Draft the three decision options" gives the hour a target. When the block ends, you can tell whether it worked. The calendar is not the win; the finished piece is.

The time-block protocol is plain: Schedule block, Define outcome, Protect from interruption, Use best energy. Emilia can check all four before she starts. No schedule means no room. No outcome means no finish. No protection means no door. Poor energy means poor work.

The overcorrection hides inside the word protected. If Blake blocks the whole week, ignores urgent handoffs, and calls every request an interruption, the method has curdled. Protected time is not a wall against responsibility. It is a fence around the work that matters most. Keep the gate, but know when to open it.

Use the block to finish meaningful work, not to look pure. Tell people what is protected, choose the task before the block begins, and count the restarts that vanish when the work gets enough room. Protected time serves the frog.

examples.title: Emilia and Blake Choose the Hour

planSpec.domain: calendar appointment with the high-value task
planSpec.audience: Emilia and Blake, two managers facing the same proposal block
planSpec.stakes: One calendar protects the frog while the other leaves the task to spare minutes.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Show the scheduled appointment with the frog as a real calendar choice with consequences.

examples.scenario: At the conference room table at 8:30, project manager Emilia opens the proposal folder and creates a 9 to 10 calendar block before her inbox loads. She treats the high-value task like a meeting with consequences and marks it protected. Across the table, Blake leaves the same proposal between four short meetings. When his first gap arrives, he is still finding the spreadsheet while Emilia is choosing the first sentence.
examples.whatToDo: Emilia treats the proposal page as an appointment with consequences, names the outcome, and starts with the file already open.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why priority needs a protected appointment. A high-value task left to gaps pays a restart cost before it can produce anything.

examples.title: Annabelle Moves the First Hour

planSpec.audience: Annabelle, a project lead who keeps losing the hard task after calls begin
planSpec.stakes: The hardest work keeps sliding behind routine demands unless the day starts differently.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Let a mentor reframe early work as protection from later interruption.

examples.scenario: On the phone before bed, Annabelle says the analysis never survives the first wave of calls and messages. Henry asks where her best hour goes. Annabelle says, "Usually to replies." Henry is quiet for a beat. "Put the frog where the world has not found you yet." Annabelle moves the analysis block before the inbox.
examples.whatToDo: Annabelle moves the analysis block before calls begin and leaves the inbox closed until the first outcome is drafted.
examples.whyItMatters: Timing can defend attention. The early block protects the hardest task before reactive demands make the calendar look already spoken for.

examples.title: Jenna Counts the Restarts

planSpec.domain: onboarding lesson on protected work blocks
planSpec.audience: Jenna, a new analyst learning why fragments do not work for complex tasks
planSpec.stakes: She thinks scattered minutes add up until the exercise shows how much time reentry consumes.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use learner confusion to teach why protected blocks need enough room and a clear outcome.

examples.scenario: In Tuesday onboarding at a training room table, new analyst Jenna is sure six short gaps can equal one work block. The instructor asks her to list the outcome and then count each restart: file, notes, decision, next step. By the fourth mark, the math feels different. The class has not learned a slogan. It has watched context vanish in pieces.
examples.whatToDo: Jenna names the outcome for the work block, counts the restarts, and sees why one protected stretch beats scattered gaps.
examples.whyItMatters: The learner's confusion makes the mechanism visible. Complex work needs continuity because files, context, decisions, and the mental model must be rebuilt after breaks.

examples.title: Yvonne Keeps the File Warm

planSpec.domain: file-heavy report with repeated setup cost
planSpec.audience: Yvonne, a consultant working through a complex client file
planSpec.stakes: Repeated setup makes each short session feel productive while little real progress happens.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Show the same file work before and after a protected block removes repeated reentry.

examples.scenario: Monday, Yvonne opens the client folder three times and spends each start finding the spreadsheet, notes, decisions, and mental model. The report grows by two weak lines. Tuesday, she clears the desk, leaves the files open, and protects one block for the recommendation. The same task feels less slippery because the setup cost is paid once.
examples.whatToDo: Yvonne clears the desk, keeps the client files open, and uses one block to draft the recommendation instead of restarting the setup three times.
examples.whyItMatters: Longer blocks reduce repeated setup cost. The reader can see how one prepared stretch keeps context alive long enough to turn into output.

examples.title: Ella Names the Boundary

planSpec.domain: protected block that other people must understand
planSpec.audience: Ella, a coordinator explaining when she is unavailable
planSpec.stakes: A private block can be broken by reasonable people who do not know it is protected.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Let the lesson emerge as two people shape the sentence that protects the block.

examples.scenario:
At the office doorway after standup, Ella has one client file under her arm and a protected block on her calendar. "If I mark it private, that should be enough," she says.
Henry shakes his head. "Private to you is invisible to us."
"So I announce it?"
"Plainly. Tell us the client file is protected until 11."
"And urgent items?"
"Send them to the thread."
examples.whatToDo: Ella tells the team the client file is protected until 11 and gives them one place for urgent items.
examples.whyItMatters: Protected time needs communication. Other people can respect the block only when they know what is closed and where true exceptions should go.

examples.title: Blake Guards the Best Block

planSpec.domain: best energy assigned to the highest-consequence task
planSpec.audience: Blake, a manager choosing what gets his clearest hour
planSpec.stakes: Easy tasks are ready to fill the best block unless he keeps the frog in view.
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use internal thought to keep the best block tied to the highest-consequence task.

examples.scenario: Blake sees the clean list first: approve expenses, answer three notes, tidy the agenda. They would feel good. The complex client decision memo sits below them, a high-value task with real consequences. He notices the trick. Best hour, best frog. He writes "three decision options" beside the block and leaves the easy list for later.
examples.whatToDo: Blake assigns his clearest hour to the client decision memo and names the outcome before touching the easy list.
examples.whyItMatters: The best block should serve the highest-consequence task. Otherwise protected time can become a comfortable home for low-value work.

questions.prompt: Two managers face the same complex proposal. One reserves a long block; the other works only in spare gaps. Which response fits the source idea best?
choices: The spare gaps can work if the proposal stays visible all day.
The long block can wait until smaller requests are cleared.
The long block helps because complex work needs continuity.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says complex work benefits from uninterrupted blocks. Spare gaps repeat the error that important work can always fit between other demands.

questions.prompt: Emilia's planner has "finish proposal" in the margin, but no reserved work period. Which diagnosis follows from that entry?
choices: The task needs calendar protection, not only a strong intention.
The task can stay unblocked if its importance is obvious.
The task should wait until the day opens by itself.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says high-value tasks require calendar protection. A margin note is a near miss because it names importance without reserving time.

questions.prompt: Jenna's training tally shows six short gaps spent reopening one report with little new text. Which reading fits the source fact?
choices: The gaps were too small for deep progress on the report.
The gaps were useful because short fragments add up evenly.
The gaps were enough because the report stayed near mind.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says short fragments may be too small for deep progress. Adding up minutes misses the reentry cost of the report.

questions.prompt: Annabelle plans to draft her analysis after routine client calls, but three mornings in a row the calls break the work apart. Which change matches the timing lesson?
choices: Use the early block before calls and messages begin.
Use the later block once routine demands are done.
Use whichever block remains after the team settles down.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says early blocks can protect work from later interruption. Waiting for routine demands lets those demands claim the day first.

questions.prompt: Yvonne starts the same client file three times: find files, rebuild context, remember decisions, then stop. Which cost is she paying?
choices: The setup steps keep the report familiar enough to restart.
The setup steps work like review before the real draft.
The setup steps consume the block before output begins.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says setup costs make repeated reentry expensive. Review can sound useful, but here the repeated setup eats the time.

questions.prompt: Blake labels a protected hour "strategy," but no one can tell what should exist at the end. Which revision follows the protocol?
choices: Keep the broad label so the hour can adapt as ideas appear.
Write the specific outcome the hour should produce.
Leave the hour open so any serious task can use it.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says a block should be tied to a specific outcome. A broad label can hide vagueness even when it sounds important.

questions.prompt: Ella blocks an hour but tells no one, then receives ordinary requests through it. Which adjustment fits the source fact?
choices: She should keep the block private so others learn its pattern.
She should tell people when the block is protected and where urgent items go.
She should answer quickly so the team still feels supported.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says other people need to know when a block is protected. Silence leaves reasonable teammates guessing that she is available.

questions.prompt: A week plan gives every morning to minor work and looks for large blocks after the small tasks clear. What is weak in the plan?
choices: The plan depends on minor work ending with enough speed.
The plan waits for large blocks instead of creating them.
The plan protects later focus by clearing minor work first.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says large blocks are created, not found. Waiting for minor work to clear gives small tasks first claim on the calendar.

questions.prompt: Emilia has her clearest hour free, three easy tasks ready, and a client decision memo with no options drafted. Where should the block go?
choices: Use it for the easiest tasks because they can be cleared cleanly.
Use it for any task that already has files open and ready.
Use it for the highest-consequence task that needs her best attention.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says the best block should go to the highest-consequence task. Ease and readiness are tempting but weaker sorting rules.

reviewCards.front: What is a protected work block in plain words?
reviewCards.back: It is a scheduled stretch long enough to make real progress on one priority task, with the outcome named and interruptions held outside it.

reviewCards.front: Why treat the frog like an appointment with consequences?
reviewCards.back: A calendar block gives the high-value task protected time before small work claims it. It becomes a meeting with consequences, not a wish.

reviewCards.front: How do setup costs make fragments weaker than they look?
reviewCards.back: Each restart makes you reload files, context, decisions, and the mental model. The minutes may add up, but the progress often does not.

reviewCards.front: What should be named before a protected block begins?
reviewCards.back: Name the outcome the block should produce. A block called strategy is cloudy; a block to draft three decision options can be checked.

reviewCards.front: How would role accountability (Ch 7) change the way you protect large blocks here?
reviewCards.back: It would send your best block to the output your role is judged by, not to nearby activity. Protect the block that moves the key result area.

reviewCards.front: Why does protected time need a short message to other people?
reviewCards.back: Other people cannot respect a block they cannot see. A short note says what is protected, when you will reply, and where urgent items belong.

implementationPlan.title: Protect the Best Block
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice giving the frog a real container. Protect the Best Block by naming the outcome, choosing your clearest stretch, and telling people when that stretch is closed. The move is visible protection for important work.

ifThenPlans.context: A high-value task is only written on a to-do list.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the task matters, then Protect the Best Block by putting the outcome on the calendar before small work fills the day.

ifThenPlans.context: A task keeps making you reload files and decisions.
ifThenPlans.plan: If reentry keeps stealing the first minutes, then Protect the Best Block and keep the files, notes, and next decision together.

ifThenPlans.context: Other people keep breaking the block with ordinary requests.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the block is invisible to others, then Protect the Best Block by sending one plain sentence about when you will reply.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, before each important task, count the files, notes, messages, and decisions you must reload. Use the highest count to name the task that needs one larger block.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, change one thing in your setup: keep one clear surface or folder for the frog's files only. Watch whether fewer restarts make the protected block easier to enter.

memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's time-block rule into a portable line.

memorableLines.text: Work blocks need a named finish line.
memorableLines.why: It keeps protected time tied to a visible outcome.
It states the boundary against overprotecting time for its own sake.
